course.title: International Relations
course.description: A balanced, non-partisan introduction to how states and other actors interact across borders - sovereignty, the major theories, power and law, trade, war and peace, diplomacy, human rights, and today's global challenges. Topics and structure are adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The prose here is original and written for self-study.

lessons.title: What international relations studies: states, sovereignty, and Westphalia

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the field of international relations examines, define the state and sovereignty, and describe why the Peace of Westphalia is treated as a turning point. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which 1648 settlement is commonly linked to the modern idea of state sovereignty? By the end you should be able to name the main actors in world politics - states, international organizations, and non-state groups - and say in a sentence what distinguishes a sovereign state from other kinds of political community. The aim is a shared vocabulary you can carry into every later lesson, so that words like state, sovereignty, and actor mean the same thing each time they appear.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: International relations is the study of how states and other actors interact across borders - through conflict, cooperation, trade, and law. The central actor is the state: a political unit with a defined territory, a permanent population, a government, and the capacity to enter relations with other states. Sovereignty is the principle that each state holds supreme authority within its own borders and recognizes no higher ruler outside them. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which ended the Thirty Years War in Europe, is often used as a marker for this system of independent, territorially bounded states, each formally equal under international law. Scholars debate how neatly history fits this label, but the Westphalian idea - territory, sovereignty, and non-interference - still shapes how the international order is described today. Alongside states, the field also studies international organizations, companies, and advocacy groups whose influence crosses national lines.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: Thucydides, writing on the Peloponnesian War, is often cited as an early observer of power and interest among rival cities. Thomas Hobbes described life without a common authority as insecure, an image later borrowed to picture relations among states. The 1648 settlement at Westphalia is the stock example of sovereign states agreeing to coexist. Modern examples make the ideas concrete: when a country controls its own tax policy, courts, and armed forces without outside permission, it is exercising sovereignty. When the United Nations admits a new member, it is recognizing that unit as a sovereign state among equals. Contested cases - territories seeking independence, or governments that cannot control their whole territory - show that sovereignty is both a legal claim and a practical capacity, and the two do not always match. Holding these examples together helps you see the field as the study of order and disorder among many separate authorities.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four common features of a state. 2) In one sentence, define sovereignty. 3) Which 1648 settlement is linked to the sovereign-state system? 4) Give one actor in world politics that is not a state. 5) Why might a government hold legal sovereignty yet lack full practical control? Answers: 1) a defined territory, a permanent population, a government, and the capacity to relate to other states. 2) the principle that a state has supreme authority within its borders and no superior outside them. 3) the Peace of Westphalia. 4) an international organization, a company, or an advocacy group (any one). 5) because sovereignty is a legal claim, while a weak or divided government may not actually govern all of its territory, so law and capacity can diverge.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating international relations as only the study of wars - it equally covers trade, law, diplomacy, and cooperation. Mistake: assuming sovereignty means a state can do anything; in practice states accept treaties and norms that limit their choices. Mistake: reading 1648 as a sharp before-and-after line rather than a convenient marker for a gradual shift that was never complete or universal. Exit: (a) What principle gives each state supreme authority at home? (b) Name one non-state actor the field studies. Answers: sovereignty; an international organization, a corporation, or an advocacy group (any one). If both come easily, you are ready to meet the theories that try to explain how these actors behave.

lessons.title: The major theories: realism, liberalism, constructivism

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compare the main theoretical lenses that scholars use to explain world politics, and match a claim to the theory most likely to make it. Warm-up: which theory stresses that the system has no central ruler and that states pursue power and security? By the end you should be able to summarize realism, liberalism, and constructivism in a sentence each, and explain briefly how Marxist or critical approaches add a focus on economic class. These lenses are not political slogans or predictions so much as sets of starting assumptions about what matters most, and learning to tell them apart will make everything that follows easier to read.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A theory in IR is a simplified lens that highlights some features of world politics and plays down others. Realism assumes the system is anarchic - no ruler above states - so states rely on their own power and pursue national interest and security, often expecting competition. Liberalism accepts anarchy but argues that institutions, trade, democracy, and interdependence let states cooperate and reduce the costs of conflict. Constructivism shifts attention from material power to ideas: it holds that interests and identities are socially constructed through norms, history, and shared beliefs, so what states want can change over time. A note on Marxist and critical approaches: they emphasize economic structures, class, and global capitalism, arguing that patterns of wealth and production shape political outcomes. No single lens is complete, so analysts often borrow from several at once.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: Hans Morgenthau gave classical realism its emphasis on interest defined as power, and Kenneth Waltz recast realism around the structure of the system. On the liberal side, writers building on Immanuel Kant stressed that republics, commerce, and international institutions can encourage peace. Alexander Wendt is closely linked to constructivism and the line that anarchy is what states make of it. For a concrete contrast: a realist might read an arms buildup as states balancing threats; a liberal might point to trade ties and institutions that raise the cost of war; a constructivist might ask how two states came to see each other as friends or enemies in the first place. A critical theorist might ask who benefits economically from the arrangement. Each reading can illuminate a different part of the same event, which is why holding more than one lens is useful.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which theory stresses anarchy, power, and national interest? 2) Which theory highlights institutions, trade, and interdependence as paths to cooperation? 3) Which theory argues that interests and identities are socially constructed? 4) What do Marxist and critical approaches emphasize? 5) Is any one theory a complete account of world politics? Answers: 1) realism. 2) liberalism. 3) constructivism. 4) economic structures, class, and global capitalism. 5) no - each lens highlights some features and omits others, so analysts often combine them rather than treating one as the whole truth.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a theory as a political opinion rather than a set of analytical assumptions - a scholar can use realism without wanting conflict. Mistake: assuming liberalism denies conflict or that realism denies cooperation; each allows both, with different emphasis. Mistake: reducing constructivism to the claim that nothing is real; it says that ideas and norms, not only material forces, shape behavior. Exit: (a) Name the theory associated with the line that anarchy is what states make of it. (b) Which approach foregrounds economic class and capitalism? Answers: constructivism; Marxist or critical approaches. If you can state each lens in a sentence, you are ready to look closely at power itself.

lessons.title: Power, the balance of power, and anarchy

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define power and anarchy as they are used in IR, and explain how a balance of power is supposed to work. Warm-up: in this field, does anarchy mean chaos and violence? By the end you should be able to distinguish hard and soft power, describe how states balance against a rising rival either by building up their own strength or by forming alliances, and explain why the absence of a world government does not automatically mean constant war. These concepts sit underneath realism in particular, but every lens has to account for how power is distributed and used.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In international relations, anarchy has a precise meaning: there is no central authority standing above sovereign states to enforce rules. It does not mean disorder or violence as everyday speech suggests - states still trade, sign treaties, and cooperate under anarchy. Power is the capacity to influence outcomes and other actors. Hard power rests on military and economic strength; soft power works through attraction, culture, and legitimacy. The balance of power is the idea that stability is more likely when no single state is strong enough to dominate the rest. States can balance internally, by increasing their own military and economic capacity, or externally, by forming alliances with others against a rising power. When balancing works, would-be dominators are checked; when it fails, one state may achieve preponderance, which others may find threatening.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: Kenneth Waltz argued that the structure of anarchy pushes states to watch relative power and to balance against concentrations of it. Classical European diplomacy offers the textbook case: coalitions repeatedly formed to check whichever state seemed poised to dominate the continent. The Cold War is often described as a bipolar balance between two large powers and their alliance blocs. Soft power, a term associated with Joseph Nye, appears when a country's ideas, education, or culture draw others toward its preferences without coercion. A simple example of balancing: if one state expands its navy, neighbors may expand theirs or band together, so that no one gains a free hand. These cases show anarchy and order coexisting - no ruler above states, yet patterns and restraint all the same.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does anarchy mean in IR? 2) Name the two broad kinds of power discussed here. 3) What are the two ways a state can balance against a rival? 4) Does anarchy guarantee constant war? 5) What is the balance of power meant to prevent? Answers: 1) the absence of a central authority above sovereign states. 2) hard power and soft power. 3) internally, by building its own strength, and externally, by forming alliances. 4) no - states still cooperate, trade, and make treaties under anarchy. 5) any single state becoming strong enough to dominate the others, which is why rivals so often combine against a rising power.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating anarchy with chaos or lawlessness; it is a structural claim about the lack of a ruler, not a prediction of violence. Mistake: thinking power is only military; economic weight and soft power also count. Mistake: assuming a balance of power is automatic - it depends on states choosing to build up or ally, and it can fail. Exit: (a) Besides building its own forces, how can a state balance a rival? (b) What kind of power works through attraction rather than force? Answers: by forming alliances with other states; soft power. With these in hand you are ready for a short checkpoint on the ground you have covered.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the main parts of the United Nations, explain what international organizations do, and say where international law comes from. Warm-up: which UN body includes five permanent members with a veto? By the end you should be able to name several UN organs, distinguish treaties from custom as sources of law, and explain why international law can bind states even without a global police force. This lesson shows how actors living under anarchy still build rules and institutions, which is the puzzle that liberal approaches in particular try to explain.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: International organizations are bodies created by states to pursue shared goals, from security to health to trade. The United Nations, founded in 1945, is the broadest. Its main organs include the General Assembly, where all members have a vote; the Security Council, charged with peace and security, whose five permanent members hold a veto; the Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General; the International Court of Justice, which settles disputes between states; and the Economic and Social Council. International law is the body of rules that states accept as binding. Its main sources are treaties, which are written agreements, and customary law, which arises from consistent state practice followed out of a sense of obligation. Because there is no world government to enforce it, international law relies on consent, reciprocity, reputation, and the work of courts and organizations.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: Hugo Grotius is often called a founder of modern international law for systematizing rules of war and peace. The UN Charter is the central treaty of the postwar order, setting out the powers of each organ. Specialized agencies give concrete examples: the World Health Organization coordinates on disease, and other bodies handle labor, refugees, and civil aviation. The International Court of Justice has ruled on border and maritime disputes between consenting states. Regional organizations also matter: the European Union pools some authority among members, while bodies such as the African Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations coordinate their regions. Enforcement varies: the Security Council can authorize sanctions or peacekeeping, but action often depends on agreement among its most powerful members, which is why the veto is so consequential and so debated.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three principal organs of the United Nations. 2) Which organ has five permanent members with a veto? 3) What are the two main sources of international law? 4) What court settles legal disputes between states at the UN? 5) Why can international law bind states without a global police force? Answers: 1) any three of the General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat, International Court of Justice, and Economic and Social Council. 2) the Security Council. 3) treaties and customary law. 4) the International Court of Justice. 5) because states consent to it and are held by reciprocity, reputation, courts, and organizations rather than by a single enforcer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the General Assembly can pass binding laws like a world parliament; most of its resolutions are recommendations. Mistake: assuming international law does not count because there is no world police; much of it is followed routinely through consent and self-interest. Mistake: confusing the International Court of Justice, which hears disputes between states, with criminal courts that try individuals. Exit: (a) Which UN organ carries primary responsibility for peace and security? (b) Name one source of international law besides treaties. Answers: the Security Council; customary law. Next you will see how states manage the economic side of their relations.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the global political economy studies, describe the basic case for trade, and define common trade tools and institutions. Warm-up: what is a tax on imported goods called? By the end you should be able to explain comparative advantage in plain terms, contrast free trade with protectionism in a balanced way, and name the main institutions that govern trade and finance across borders. The goal is not to argue for one trade policy, but to equip you to read debates in which reasonable people weigh real trade-offs between efficiency and other values.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Global political economy studies how politics and economics interact across borders - how states, markets, and institutions shape trade, money, and development. A core idea is comparative advantage: countries gain when each specializes in what it produces relatively most efficiently and then trades, expanding total output. Governments influence trade with tools such as tariffs, which are taxes on imports, quotas, which cap quantities, and subsidies, which support domestic producers. Free-trade arguments stress lower prices, variety, and efficiency; protectionist arguments stress safeguarding jobs, new industries, or strategic sectors. Both views have real trade-offs, and most countries mix them. Key institutions include the World Trade Organization, which sets trade rules and hears disputes, the International Monetary Fund, which lends to countries in financial trouble, and the World Bank, which funds development. Together they form much of the architecture of the world economy.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in the early nineteenth century, showing that trade can benefit both partners even when one is better at making everything. Adam Smith earlier argued that specialization and exchange raise prosperity. A simple illustration: if one country makes cloth cheaply and another makes wine cheaply, both gain by specializing and trading rather than making both alone. Modern examples include regional trade agreements that lower tariffs among members, and disputes brought to the World Trade Organization when one state accuses another of unfair barriers. The International Monetary Fund has provided emergency loans during financial crises, often attaching policy conditions that are themselves debated. These cases show economics and politics entwined: trade creates aggregate gains, but the gains and costs fall unevenly, which is why trade policy is so contested.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a tariff? 2) State the idea of comparative advantage in one sentence. 3) Name one argument for free trade and one for protection. 4) Which institution sets trade rules and hears trade disputes? 5) What does the International Monetary Fund mainly do? Answers: 1) a tax on imported goods. 2) countries gain by specializing in what they produce relatively most efficiently and trading for the rest. 3) free trade: lower prices and efficiency; protection: safeguarding jobs or strategic industries (any valid pair). 4) the World Trade Organization. 5) it lends to countries facing financial or balance-of-payments trouble.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating trade as a win-only or lose-only matter; it tends to raise total output while distributing gains and costs unevenly. Mistake: confusing a tariff, which is a tax on imports, with a quota, which is a limit on quantity. Mistake: assuming comparative advantage requires being the best at something; it only requires being relatively more efficient. Exit: (a) What trade tool caps the quantity of an import? (b) Name the institution that funds development projects. Answers: a quota; the World Bank. Keeping the efficiency gains and the distribution of costs both in view is the mark of a balanced reading.

lessons.title: War and peace, security, diplomacy, and foreign policy

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define security, deterrence, diplomacy, and foreign policy, and explain how states try to prevent war and manage disputes short of it. Warm-up: what does it mean to deter an attack? By the end you should be able to describe deterrence and alliances, explain the purpose of diplomacy, and say in a sentence what foreign policy is and who makes it. The focus is on how states pursue safety and their goals without, where possible, resorting to force, and on the tools that keep disputes from escalating into armed conflict.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Security studies asks how states protect themselves and reduce the risk of war. Deterrence means discouraging an attack by convincing an opponent that the costs of attacking would outweigh any gains, usually through the credible threat of retaliation. Alliances pool strength so that an attack on one is treated as a concern for all. Diplomacy is the practice of managing relations between states through negotiation, communication, and representation; diplomats gather information, signal intentions, and bargain to settle differences peacefully. Foreign policy is the set of goals and strategies a government adopts toward other states and the world - decisions about trade, alliances, aid, and the use of force. It is shaped by leaders, bureaucracies, domestic politics, and public opinion. Together these tools aim to secure a state's interests while lowering the chance that disputes escalate into armed conflict.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: Carl von Clausewitz famously described war as a continuation of policy by other means, linking force to political aims. Thomas Schelling analyzed deterrence and bargaining, showing how threats and signals can shape behavior without fighting. The concept of mutual deterrence featured heavily in the Cold War, when two heavily armed blocs sought to avoid direct war. Alliances such as collective-defense pacts illustrate the pooling of security. Diplomacy appears whenever states negotiate a cease-fire, a trade deal, or an arms-control treaty, often through embassies and summits. Foreign policy examples include a government deciding whether to join an alliance, impose sanctions, or send humanitarian aid. These cases show a spectrum from cooperation to conflict, with diplomacy and deterrence as the main tools states use to stay on the peaceful end of it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Define deterrence in one sentence. 2) What is the purpose of an alliance? 3) What is diplomacy? 4) What is foreign policy, and name one actor who shapes it. 5) Give one tool states use to settle disputes without fighting. Answers: 1) discouraging an attack by threatening costs that would outweigh any gains. 2) to pool strength so that an attack on one member concerns all. 3) managing relations between states through negotiation, communication, and representation. 4) a government's goals and strategies toward other states, shaped by leaders, bureaucracies, or public opinion (any one). 5) negotiation, treaties, mediation, or summits (any one).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating security only with military force; economic, energy, and other dimensions also count. Mistake: thinking deterrence requires using force - it works precisely by threatening costs so that force is not used. Mistake: treating diplomacy as weakness; it is a primary instrument for advancing interests and avoiding war. Exit: (a) What is an alliance meant to achieve? (b) What is the main goal of deterrence? Answers: to pool strength so an attack on one concerns all members; to prevent an attack by making its costs outweigh its gains. These tools set up the harder debates about rights and intervention that come next.

lessons.title: Human rights, intervention, and contemporary global issues

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the idea of human rights in world politics, describe the debate over humanitarian intervention, and outline major contemporary global issues. Warm-up: which 1948 document set out a shared list of human rights? By the end you should be able to summarize the tension between sovereignty and human rights, state both sides of the intervention debate fairly, and name current challenges such as globalization, climate diplomacy, and nuclear proliferation. These are live questions on which thoughtful people disagree, so the aim is to represent each position accurately rather than to settle them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Human rights are claims said to belong to all people simply by virtue of being human, such as life, liberty, and freedom from torture. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 set out a widely cited list, later developed in binding treaties. In world politics this creates tension with sovereignty: if a government abuses its own people, do other states have a right or a duty to act? Humanitarian intervention is the use of pressure, or sometimes force, to protect people in another state from grave harm. Supporters argue there is a responsibility to protect when a government cannot or will not; critics warn that intervention can be misused, cause harm, or violate sovereignty and be applied inconsistently. Contemporary issues cut across borders: globalization ties economies and cultures together, climate diplomacy seeks shared action on a shared atmosphere, and the spread of nuclear weapons, or proliferation, raises enduring security concerns.

sections.heading: Key thinkers & examples
sections.text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, shaped by a drafting committee that included Eleanor Roosevelt, is the reference point for later covenants on civil, political, economic, and social rights. The principle known as the responsibility to protect, endorsed at a UN summit, tries to balance sovereignty with the prevention of mass atrocities. Debates over past interventions show the difficulty: some are credited with halting atrocities, while others are criticized for unintended consequences or inconsistent application. On global issues, climate diplomacy appears in agreements where states set emissions pledges, and non-proliferation efforts center on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and inspections by international agencies. Globalization is visible in supply chains, migration, and the rapid movement of information. These examples share a theme: problems that no single state can solve alone, pushing states toward cooperation even under anarchy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What are human rights, in one sentence? 2) Which 1948 document listed them? 3) What is humanitarian intervention? 4) State one argument for and one against intervention. 5) Name two contemporary global issues that cross borders. Answers: 1) claims said to belong to all people simply because they are human. 2) the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 3) the use of pressure or force to protect people in another state from grave harm. 4) for: a responsibility to protect against atrocities; against: risk of misuse, harm, or violating sovereignty (any valid pair). 5) any two of globalization, climate diplomacy, and nuclear proliferation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the sovereignty-versus-human-rights question as having an easy answer; thoughtful people disagree, and the tension is real. Mistake: assuming intervention is always either purely noble or purely cynical; outcomes and motives vary case by case. Mistake: thinking global issues like climate or proliferation can be handled by one state alone. Exit: (a) What principle tries to balance sovereignty with preventing mass atrocities? (b) What does proliferation refer to here? Answers: the responsibility to protect; the spread of nuclear weapons. A fair summary states each side on its own strongest terms.
